title: Does arithmetic formula hardness derandomize identity testing?
formal: Does \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\) hold over \(\mathbb Q\)? Here \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\) asserts that there exists an explicit family \(f_m\in\mathbb Q[x_1,\ldots,x_m]\) of multilinear polynomials with \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\), in the precise sense below. The assertion \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) is that, for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), polynomial identity testing for unrestricted arithmetic formulas has a uniform deterministic algorithm taking time \(2^{O(N^{\varepsilon})}\), where \(N\) is the input's bit length. This card selects the hardness-to-derandomization branch of the source's two-direction question; it asks for subexponential time, without requiring polynomial time.

source_formulation.text: For example, does super-polynomial lower bounds for arithmetic formulas imply non-trivial deterministic algorithms for PIT for arithmetic formulas, and vice-versa?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 3

why: This asks whether hardness against arithmetic computation without shared subexpressions already suffices to remove randomness from identity testing in that same fundamental model. A resolution would clarify whether the central circuit hardness–randomness principle survives the restriction to formulas, connecting algebraic lower bounds with deterministic symbolic computation.
status_note: The selected forward branch is explicitly motivated by the 2018 source and repeated in its 2019 journal version; a 2019 survey also poses a stronger polynomial-time version. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026 found no verified resolution of the stated unrestricted-formula implication. The checked 2025 uniform-network and border-determinant results, and the 2026 read-4 algorithm, have materially different hypotheses or models. This records bounded review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The source quotation retains its original two-direction wording; the formal target explicitly selects the forward subexponential branch.

progress.text: Kabanets and Impagliazzo prove the general-circuit forward tradeoff and a Boolean-or-algebraic lower-bound consequence of derandomizing formula PIT.
Chou, Kumar and Solomon state the unrestricted-formula question while proving a conditional PIT result for bounded-depth circuits using a low-degree hardness hypothesis.
The expanded journal paper repeats the formula question and gives the exact coefficient-list explicitness definition used here.
Andrews, Kush and Tell give a polynomial-time PIT equivalence for uniform arithmetic networks under a different, almost-all-inputs hardness condition.
Andrews constructs a generator for polynomial-size formulas under a specific border-formula lower bound for the determinant.
Kaplan and Shpilka obtain polynomial-time white-box and quasipolynomial-time black-box PIT for read-4 formulas, a restricted subclass of the target model.

importance.reason: A central structural question joining algebraic formula lower bounds to derandomization in the same computation model. It probes the scope of a foundational hardness–randomness principle and has consequences for deterministic polynomial identity testing beyond a narrow circuit subclass. The score reflects this broad conceptual reach, not the venue or the former provisional midpoint.

sentences: An arithmetic formula is a tree of additions and multiplications with rational constants and commuting variables.
Assume a coefficient-explicit multilinear polynomial family eventually requires formulas larger than every fixed polynomial in its variable count.
Must there then be deterministic identity testers for every unrestricted formula in time 2^{O(N^epsilon)} for every epsilon > 0?
The selected target is the forward, subexponential branch of the original two-direction question.
Known later results change the hardness assumption or restrict the formula model; the bounded review found no verified resolution of this implication.

definitions:
An arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb Q\) is a finite rooted binary tree. Each leaf is labeled by a rational constant or a variable, and each internal node by addition or multiplication. It computes its polynomial in commuting variables by the indicated operations; there are no division or exponentiation gates and no shared internal subcomputations. Negative rational constants are allowed. Its size is its number of edges. Let \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f)\) be the minimum size among formulas computing exactly \(f\). Rational constants of arbitrary bit length are permitted in this minimum, and their bit lengths are not charged to this algebraic size. The lower bound is against every formula, with no depth, read-count, homogeneity or intermediate multilinearity restriction. A polynomial is multilinear when each variable has exponent at most one in every monomial. Explicitness of \((f_m)_{m\ge1}\) means that there are positive integers \(a,b,C\) and one deterministic Turing machine which, on unary input \(1^m\), outputs the ordered list of all \(2^m\) rational coefficients of \(f_m\) in time at most \(2^{a m+C}\), and every coefficient has numerator/denominator bit length at most \(C(m+1)^b\). The order is lexicographic on exponent vectors in \(\{0,1\}^m\); zero coefficients are included. Coefficients are written as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator in reduced form. The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)=m^{\omega(1)}\) means \(\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}\ \exists m_0\ \forall m\ge m_0:\ L_{\mathrm{form}}(f_m)>m^k\). Thus the hard family is uniform in its coefficient generation, while the competing formulas are nonuniform. For PIT the input is an arbitrary formula, with its tree and gate labels explicitly supplied, variable indices in binary, and rational constants in binary numerator/denominator form. Use the following prefix encoding. For a nonnegative integer \(r\), let \(\ell\) be the bit length of \(r+1\) and write \(\ell\) one-bits, one zero-bit and the \(\ell\)-bit binary representation of \(r+1\). A signed integer \(p\) is represented by this code for \(2p\) when \(p\ge0\), and for \(-2p-1\) otherwise. A rational is its signed-numerator code followed by its positive-denominator code, with numerator and denominator coprime. The four two-bit formula tags are 00 for a rational leaf (followed by that rational code), 01 for a variable leaf (followed by its positive integer index), 10 for addition and 11 for multiplication. Each internal-node tag is followed recursively by the encodings of its left and right children. No trailing bits are permitted. Let \(N\) be the total encoding length. The hard-family coefficient list uses the same rational encoding, concatenated in the specified order. The required output is whether the computed formal polynomial has every coefficient zero. The tester may examine the formula description (white-box access); a black-box hitting-set construction is not required. There is no promise that the input computes a multilinear polynomial. Time is measured in bit operations of a deterministic Turing machine, including reading constants, and the tester uses neither randomness nor advice nor an oracle. More precisely, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there must be a machine \(A_\varepsilon\), constants \(c_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon>0\), and a threshold \(N_\varepsilon\) such that it is correct on every valid formula and takes at most \(C_\varepsilon 2^{c_\varepsilon N^\varepsilon}\) steps on every formula of length \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). Machines and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on the input. The implication concerns existence of these algorithms; it does not additionally require a uniform compiler from descriptions of hard families to testers.

For the stated bit costs, a deterministic multitape Turing machine has one read-only input tape, finitely many initially blank work tapes, fixed finite control and alphabet, and one head on each tape. One transition reads the symbols under the heads, changes state, writes at most one symbol on each work tape and moves each head by at most one cell; it may append at most one output bit. Each transition costs one. Tape cells are indexed by nonnegative integers and a left move at zero stays there. The program and tape count are independent of input length. Malformed encodings may be rejected; correctness and the displayed clocks are required on every valid encoded instance.
answer_criterion:
Give a mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the full implication \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\Rightarrow D_{\mathrm{form}}\), or a Lean-checked refutation establishing \(H_{\mathrm{form}}\land\neg D_{\mathrm{form}}\) under exactly the definitions above. A positive answer must cover unrestricted rational arithmetic formulas and every \(\varepsilon>0\). A result assuming lower bounds against general circuits, exponential formula hardness, a particular stronger border-complexity hypothesis, or hardness only for an additionally constrained polynomial family does not by itself prove this implication. A restricted-depth, bounded-read or noncommutative PIT algorithm alone is insufficient. This is a logical implication; proving the hard-family hypothesis unconditionally is not required for a positive answer.

Equivalently, failure of \(D_{\mathrm{form}}\) means there is an \(\varepsilon>0\) such that, for every uniform deterministic machine \(A\) that halts with the correct PIT answer on every valid formula, all positive constants \(c,C\), and every length threshold \(N_0\), there is a valid formula \(F\) of encoding length \(N\ge N_0\) on which \(A\) takes more than \(C2^{cN^\varepsilon}\) transitions. A refutation must establish this failure together with the hard-family hypothesis.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 source asks about both directions between formula lower bounds and nontrivial deterministic PIT. The chosen branch tests whether the usual superpolynomial hardness-to-subexponential-time principle for circuits also holds for formulas. The source's formal coefficient-list definition supplies the explicitness condition used here.

For general arithmetic circuits, Kabanets and Impagliazzo establish the corresponding forward tradeoff: superpolynomial hardness of an explicit multilinear family gives deterministic PIT in time with arbitrarily small positive powers in the exponent. A stronger hardness assumption gives quasipolynomial time. Circuit hardness is a stronger hypothesis than formula hardness.

The reverse direction depends on how the tester accesses its input. A black-box hitting set is a finite set of evaluation points on which every nonzero polynomial in the specified formula class is nonzero somewhere. Such constructions imply algebraic lower bounds. An arbitrary white-box tester need not provide a hitting set. The known white-box formula-PIT consequence in Kabanets–Impagliazzo is a disjunction: either a nondeterministic exponential-time language has no polynomial-size Boolean circuits, or the permanent has no polynomial-size division-free integer arithmetic formulas. It is not stated as the converse of this card's single explicit-family hypothesis.
The 2019 survey explicitly poses a stronger forward formula question with a polynomial-time conclusion. The present target retains the weaker subexponential conclusion from the 2018 question.

The 2025 polynomial-time PIT equivalence uses hardness against uniform arithmetic networks with PIT gates on almost all individual inputs. Its model and hardness condition differ from the nonuniform formula-size hypothesis here.

Another 2025 theorem gives a hitting-set generator for formulas assuming a stronger, specific lower bound: superpolynomial border-formula complexity of the determinant. Border complexity permits polynomials arising as limits of computations, and its lower bound is not supplied merely by the hypothesis in this card.
The 2026 read-4 result supplies deterministic PIT algorithms when each variable occurs at most four times in a formula. The target here permits an unbounded number of occurrences and arbitrary depth.

checked_sources: The source's unrestricted-formula sentence is different from its numbered Question 1 about bounded-depth circuits. Theorem 3 does not answer the general formula question. Retain ordinary commutative rational formulas of unrestricted depth and variable reuse; do not silently move to multilinear formulas, bounded-read formulas, ABPs, noncommutative formulas or a general circuit lower-bound hypothesis.

Quantifier recovery: CCC 2018 p. 13:2 footnote 3 explicitly points to subexponential versus quasipolynomial time depending on hardness. Its referenced KI 2004 Theorem 7.7, visually checked on pp. 36–37, states s_p(m) in m^{omega(1)} and time 2^{n^epsilon} for every epsilon > 0; the stronger 2^{m^{Omega(1)}} hardness gives quasipolynomial time. Thus the proposed formula analogue uses almost-everywhere superpolynomial growth, not merely an infinitely-often failure of membership in a polynomial-size class. This is an explicit recovery of the cited tradeoff, not a claim that the informal 2018 sentence itself writes all these quantifiers.

Explicitness follows CCC 2018 Definition 10 (p. 13:8), confirmed by journal 2019 Definition 4.7 (p. 12): all coefficient bit lengths are polynomial, and all 2^m coefficients are listed in 2^{O(m)} time. Do not replace this with the stronger per-coefficient polynomial-time condition suggested by an informal journal introduction footnote. Restricting to Q follows the paper's setup; no extension to every field is demanded. Multilinearity applies to the hypothetical hard polynomial family only, not to the circuits that are lower-bounded or the PIT inputs.

Algebraic hardness size counts wires and permits arbitrary rational constants without charging their bit lengths, matching the source's circuit convention. Binary fan-in is a harmless normalization: each unbounded-fan-in formula gate can be replaced by a binary tree with only linear size change. Rational signs can be represented by constants. There is no division or compressed power operation. PIT is a conventional white-box decision problem on the full finite formula description; its bit cost includes constants. Its bit length and reasonable alternative prefix encodings are polynomially related, which leaves membership in the intersection over all epsilon > 0 of DTIME(2^{N^epsilon}) invariant.

The source's displayed bounded-depth runtime is expressed in variables, size and degree. For an explicitly supplied formula, degree and number of distinct variables are at most linear in its tree size, while all input coefficient bits are part of N. The proposed total-bit-length SUBEXP formulation is the ordinary decision-language version of the selected nontrivial runtime regime. It does not demand subexponential complexity independently of arbitrarily large input coefficient encodings or a polynomial-time algorithm. Each epsilon may have a different uniform deterministic machine; no input-length advice, oracle or random coins are allowed.

The existence implication deliberately does not add an effective uniform compiler accepting the generator of any hard family or a proof of its lower bound. The mathematical family is uniform through its coefficient-list algorithm; its lower bound applies to nonuniform formulas. A positive proof is conditional on H and need not construct an unconditional superpolynomial lower bound. A negative proof must establish H and failure of the full D, not merely failure of a particular generator construction.

The saved 'vice-versa' cannot automatically be read as D iff exactly H. KI 2004 Theorem 4.9, visually inspected on p. 25, excludes simultaneous NEXP subset P/poly, polynomial-size division-free integer formulas for permanent, and infinitely-often nondeterministic SUBEXP AFIT. It gives a Boolean-or-arithmetic disjunction, not H alone. Black-box hitting sets give algebraic hardness by a different theorem; a general white-box tester need not output a hitting set. The 2019 survey distinguishes these issues in Sections 3.1–3.2, PDF pp. 7–9. The forward selection preserves a genuine explicitly sourced branch without silently asserting a stronger equivalence.

Kumar–Saptharishi 2019 Question 4.14 (PDF p. 21, repeated pp. 29–30) asks the stronger polynomial-time forward question. It corroborates the significance of the formula branch but does not authorize replacing this card's original nontrivial/subexponential target by polynomial time. That survey is used as a primary source for its own open-question formulation, not as a substitute for checking the newer theorem statements.

Bounded later review: actual 2025 TR25-042 Theorems 1.2–1.3, printed p. 3/PDF p. 5, use strongly uniform circuits and uniform arithmetic networks with PIT gates, together with hardness on every sufficiently late individual input. This is materially different from H. Actual CCC 2025 Theorem 1.2, p. 15:7, assumes superpolynomial border-formula complexity specifically of determinant; p. 15:8 emphasizes this distinction. No PIT runtime is inferred just from a generator's existence or a small stretch. Actual TR26-076 abstract and Section 1.1 concern read-4 only. A bounded ECCC PIT-index check and targeted primary searches through the review date found no matching full theorem; this is not exhaustive status certification.

CCC 2025 publication was 29 July, not the arXiv submission date; ECCC read-4 report date and publication timestamp differ by one day and both are recorded.

Importance was genuinely unassessed at 50. Recommend 90 independently for the forward branch: it asks whether a foundational correspondence survives the difference between circuits and formulas, coupling two major themes with broad implications for symbolic computation. Preserve the existing category. This is a yes/no conditional implication, so numerical 1/100 acceptance and asymptotic-curve approximation do not apply.
